primer.title: Errors are values; ? passes them up
body: A fallible function returns `Result<T, E>`. `expr?` unwraps `Ok(v)` to `v`, or **returns** `Err(From::from(e))` from the enclosing function.
Two consequences worth reading for: `?` only works inside a function that itself returns `Result` (or `Option`), and the error must be convertible with `From` into that function's error type.
When no `From` impl exists, convert explicitly first:
`Box<dyn Error>` accepts any error type, because the standard library implements `From<E> for Box<dyn Error>` for every `E: Error`.

verify.stdout:
Ok(171)
error: invalid digit found in string

code: error: invalid digit found in string
options.rationale: `?` returns the `ParseIntError` to the caller instead of panicking. `{:?}` on a `Result` prints the `Ok(…)` wrapper too.

code: error: invalid digit found in string
options.rationale: `total_cost` returns a `Result`, and Debug-printing it shows the variant: `Ok(171)`.
A failed `parse` does not yield 0. `?` leaves the function at line 6, so line 8 never runs.
`?` is the opposite of `unwrap`: it hands the error back as a value.

exercises.prompt: This does not compile. What does the compiler object to?

options.text: E0277: `?` on line 10 needs a function that returns `Result` or `Option`, but `main` returns `()`
options.rationale: `?` may have to return an `Err`, and `main` has no way to return one. `fn main() -> Result<(), ParseIntError>` fixes it.

options.text: E0277: `?` on line 4 cannot be used with `parse`
options.rationale: Line 4 is fine: `total_cost` returns `Result<i32, ParseIntError>`, exactly what `parse::<i32>()` can fail with.

options.text: E0308: `cost` is a `Result`, which cannot be compared with `tokens`
options.rationale: If line 10 compiled, `?` would already have unwrapped it to an `i32`.

options.text: It compiles and prints `You now have 59 tokens.`
options.rationale: That is what it would print once `main` returned a `Result`. As written, line 10 is rejected.
Arms are tried top to bottom. The guard catches -3, the literal `0` catches zero, and only then does the catch-all `x` run.
That is what `-3 as u64` would give — but the guarded first arm catches negatives before the cast is reached.
Derived `Debug` prints a tuple struct with its name: `Positive(10)`.

options.text: It does not compile: the arms `x if x < 0` and `x` overlap
options.rationale: Overlapping patterns are allowed; the first matching arm wins. Only *unreachable* arms get a warning.

verify.stdout:
ok 42
err: 7 is too small
err: invalid digit found in string

code: err: invalid digit found in string
options.rationale: `Box<dyn Error>` can hold both error types. `?` boxes the `ParseIntError` automatically; `{e}` uses each error's own `Display`.

options.text: It does not compile: `?` cannot convert `ParseIntError` into `Box<dyn Error>`
options.rationale: It can: the standard library implements `From<E> for Box<dyn Error>` for every `E: Error`. (For a `String` error type this *would* fail.)

code: err: invalid digit found in string
options.rationale: `{e}` uses `Display`, which is the hand-written `fmt`. `TooSmall(7)` is what `{e:?}` would print.

code: err: invalid digit found in string
options.rationale: 7 parses fine, but then fails the `n < 10` check on line 16.

exercises.prompt: Tap the line the compiler rejects.
code: let why = format!("{x} is not positive");
exercises.rationale: On line 10 `?` must turn a `ParseIntError` into a `ParseError`, and no `From<ParseIntError> for ParseError` exists (E0277). `.map_err(ParseError::ParseInt)?` would convert it explicitly.

lineRationales.6: Having a variant that *can* hold a `ParseIntError` is not enough — `?` only uses `From`, and nobody implemented it.
lineRationales.13: Building and returning your own variant directly needs no conversion at all.
lineRationales.9: The signature is fine. It is what obliges line 10 to produce a `ParseError`.

exercises.fallbackRationale: That line compiles. Look for a `?` whose error type differs from the function's error type.

exercises.prompt: Which replacement for the highlighted lines keeps the behaviour identical?

options.rationale: `map_err` converts `ParseIntError` into `String`, and `?` returns early on `Err` — exactly what the `match` did.
`?` needs `From<ParseIntError> for String`, which does not exist. This fails to compile.
Compiles, but bad input now becomes port 0 and is reported as `reserved`.
Turns a recoverable error into a panic.
